title: Evaluation datasets and frameworks
task_statement: Build an eval set that covers real task traffic and grade it with the cheapest reliable grader. (Inference: wording from secondary sources)

components.name: Evaluation dataset design
components.first_principle: An eval set measures the system well only when its cases match the real task distribution.

nodes.label: Edge cases: empty, long, or unclear input

steps: Sample cases from the real task distribution.
Add edge cases such as irrelevant input, empty input, and very long input.
Add ambiguous cases where even humans would struggle to agree.
Write expected answers so that code can grade most cases.
Version the set and add new cases when the task changes. (Inference)
pros: Edge cases expose failures that clean samples hide.
Automated scores make each run cheap and frequent. (Inference)
The docs say more questions with lower signal beat fewer hand-graded questions.
cons: A set misses traffic that it never sampled. (Inference)
Expected answers take effort to write and maintain. (Inference)
Shared eval cases can leak into training data. (Inference)
use_when: The application handles varied user input.
Production shows failures that a clean set does not show.
A team needs a regression check before each release.
do_not_use_when: A one-off demo has no decision attached to the result. (Inference)
The task has no real traffic yet, so the set would only reflect guesses. (Inference)

constraints.choice: Assign a domain expert to review the ambiguous cases. (Inference)
Prioritize volume with automated checks over small hand-graded sets.
constraints.combination: Add a human-graded slice for ambiguous cases. (Inference)

constraints.choice: Refresh the set when the task distribution changes. (Inference)
constraints.combination: Keep the old version so that results remain comparable. (Inference)

constraints.choice: Remove personal data from cases before they leave the trust boundary. (Inference)

components.exam_tie: D4.2. Expect a scenario where a clean test set reports a high score and production fails on unusual input. The credited answer adds edge and adversarial cases to the set. (Inference)
components.trap: A set built only from easy, clean examples. The score is high, but it does not predict production behavior.
components.decision_rule: Build the eval set from production traffic, and add edge cases that production contains.
components.exam_tip: A high average on a clean set does not prove the system handles the hard cases.

components.name: Graders for evaluations
components.first_principle: Use the cheapest grader that stays reliable for each type of case.

nodes.label: Code grader: exact or string match
LLM grader with rubric on Claude

steps: Use a code grader first for exact match and string match checks.
Use an LLM grader for judgment that code cannot express.
Write a detailed rubric with a clear pass condition and a fixed output format.
Turn on thinking for the grader model when the judgment is complex.
Test the LLM grader for reliability before you scale it.
Use a human grader only when the other methods cannot decide.
pros: The docs rank code graders as the fastest and most reliable method.
An LLM grader handles subtle judgment at scale.
A fixed output format makes grader scores easy to parse.
cons: Code graders lack nuance for complex judgment.
Human graders are slow and expensive, so the docs say to avoid them when possible.
An LLM grader can disagree with human graders on hard cases. (Inference)
use_when: Outputs have an answer that code can check with an exact or string match.
The judgment is complex and hard to express in code.
A new LLM grader must match a reviewed sample of human labels. (Inference)
do_not_use_when: The LLM grader has not passed a reliability test on the case type. (Inference)
A human panel must grade every release at high volume. (Inference)

constraints.choice: Use code to check most cases, and reserve LLM graders for judgment.
constraints.combination: Use the Message Batches API for offline grader runs.

constraints.choice: Test each grader before it scores a release.
constraints.combination: Recheck the grader when the grader model changes. (Inference)

constraints.choice: Use reviewed human labels as the reference for each LLM grader. (Inference)
Scale LLM graders only after the reliability test passes.
constraints.combination: Use code graders for volume, because the docs call them extremely scalable.

components.exam_tie: D4.2. Expect a scenario with a cost limit and a judgment task. The credited answer uses code for checkable cases and tests an LLM grader before it scales. (Inference)
components.trap: An LLM grader that runs on every case with no reliability test. The cost is low, but the scores may be wrong.
components.decision_rule: Assign each case type the cheapest grader that passed a reliability test on that type.
components.exam_tip: Human graders are the costliest rung, so they fit only the cases that code and LLM graders cannot decide.

flowchart TD
  A{Output has a checkable answer?} -->|Yes| B[Code grader with exact or string match]
  A -->|No| C{Judgment fits a rubric?}
  C -->|Yes| D{LLM grader passed reliability test?}
  D -->|Yes| E[LLM grader with rubric]
  D -->|No| F[Human grader on a sample]
  C -->|No| F
cheatsheet:
flowchart LR
  S[Eval set] --> M[Mirror real traffic]
  M --> E[Edge cases]
  E --> V[Versioned set]
  S --> G1[Code grader: cheapest]
  S --> G2[LLM grader: rubric]
  G2 --> R[Reliability test first]
  S --> G3[Human grader: costliest]
